title: What is Money? A Short History of Currency and the Modern Financial System

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Sato
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to ask a deceptively simple question: what is money? And why is the answer to this question more surprising, and more important, than it might seem?

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Sato
dialogue.text: Money, in any economy, performs three functions. It is a medium of exchange — it enables people to trade goods and services without the inefficiency of barter. It is a store of value — it allows people to save purchasing power over time. And it is a unit of account — it provides a common standard for measuring and comparing the value of different goods. These three functions are the definition of money, regardless of the physical form it takes.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Sato
dialogue.text: The physical form of money has changed dramatically throughout history. Early money took the form of commodities — grain, cattle, salt, precious metals. The advantage of commodity money is that it has intrinsic value — gold is valuable even if no one accepts it as money. The disadvantage is that it is heavy, divisible with difficulty, and limited in supply in ways that can constrain economic activity.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Sato
dialogue.text: Paper money emerged as a form of representative money — notes that could be exchanged for a specified quantity of a commodity, typically gold or silver. The gold standard, under which currencies were pegged to gold at a fixed rate, governed international monetary arrangements for most of the nineteenth century and into the twentieth. It was abandoned during and after the Second World War, and replaced with the Bretton Woods system, in which currencies were pegged to the US dollar, which was itself convertible to gold. In 1971, the US severed this link, creating the system of "fiat money" that exists today.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Sato
dialogue.text: Fiat money is money by government decree — it has no intrinsic value and is not backed by a commodity. It is accepted as money because governments declare it legal tender and because everyone else accepts it. This might seem fragile — and in a sense it is: the value of fiat money depends entirely on confidence in the issuing authority. When that confidence collapses, as it has in several historical cases of hyperinflation, the currency can become worthless very rapidly.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Sato
dialogue.text: Most money in modern economies is not even physical. It exists as digital entries in bank records. When you deposit money in a bank, the bank does not store your notes in a vault — it lends most of them out again, keeping only a small reserve. This is the principle of "fractional reserve banking." The money supply in a modern economy is therefore a multiple of the actual physical currency in circulation — most money is created by the lending activities of commercial banks, not by governments printing notes.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Sato
dialogue.text: Central banks — like the Federal Reserve in the US, the European Central Bank, or the Bank of England — exist to manage this system. They set interest rates, which influence the cost and availability of borrowing throughout the economy. They act as "lenders of last resort" — providing liquidity to banks that cannot meet their obligations during financial crises. And they regulate the money supply in ways designed to maintain price stability — avoiding both inflation, which erodes the value of savings, and deflation, which can be equally damaging to economic activity.
